column2: Diagnostic imaging helps clinicians visualize anatomy and evaluate disease or injury. Radiographers combine patient care, accurate positioning, exposure selection, and image evaluation. Remember the workflow: verify the patient, explain the exam, position accurately, expose safely, and evaluate the image before the patient leaves.

Atoms contain protons and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons arranged in shells around it. Ionization means an electron is completely removed. Excitation means an electron moves to a higher energy level but stays in the atom. Inner-shell vacancies are especially important because they can lead to characteristic x-ray production.

The cathode is the negative side of the x-ray tube. Its heated filament releases electrons by thermionic emission, and the focusing cup directs them toward the target. The anode is the positive side. It receives the electrons at the focal spot, where most energy becomes heat and a small amount becomes x-rays.

X-rays are produced when fast electrons from the cathode strike the tungsten target. Bremsstrahlung occurs when an electron is slowed or deflected near the nucleus. Characteristic radiation begins when an incoming electron removes an inner-shell electron, and a higher-shell electron fills the vacancy, releasing a photon.

Think of kVp and mAs as two different controls. kVp primarily changes photon energy and penetration. mAs primarily changes the number of x-ray photons produced. Increasing mAs increases receptor exposure in a direct relationship. Changing kVp affects penetration and also influences receptor exposure, so technique changes should be made thoughtfully.

ALARA means keeping radiation exposure as low as reasonably achievable while still obtaining the necessary diagnostic information. The three classic protection principles are time, distance, and shielding. Reduce unnecessary beam-on time, increase distance from the source of scatter, and use appropriate barriers or protective equipment according to policy.
